title: Prognostic value of valve calcification and high cardiothoracic ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events and mortality in hemodialysis patients

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:

【Introduction · S0001-p3】VC impairs leaflet motion, obstructs blood flow, and leads to LVH, which may in turn elevate the CTR [10]. In patients undergoing MHD, LVH may contribute to or aggravate VC due to increased circulatory stress during hemodialysis, which in turn promotes greater endotoxemia, more severe inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction [11]. Compared to the general population, ESKD patients have a significantly higher prevalence of VC and cardiomegaly [12]. Furthermore, VC and LVH are known to exacerbate each other, with a longitudinal interaction that elevates the risk of mortality and CV events in ESKD patients [11]. Despite the well-established link between VC, LVH, and CV risk, limited research has explored the combined predictive value of VC and CTR for clinical outcomes in this population. Therefore, this exploratory study aimed to investigate the combined prognostic value of VC and CTR for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), CV and overall mortality in MHD patients.

【Introduction · S0001-p1】Valve calcification (VC) is characterized by the gradual fibro-calcific remodeling and thickening of the valve leaflets [1]. The pathophysiology of VC is complex, influenced by traditional risk factors such as age, sex, smoking, and comorbidities like hypertension or diabetes mellitus. In patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), inflammation, malnutrition, and calcium-phosphorus metabolism disorders play significant roles in vascular or soft tissue calcification. The prevalence of VC among ESKD patients is approximately 31.7%, with risk factors including long dialysis vintages, elevated serum calcium level, high blood pressure, diabetes, and reduced serum albumin level [2]. Aortic VC leads to left ventricular outflow obstruction, increasing ventricular workload and oxygen consumption and ultimately causing myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis, while mitral VC causes dilation of the left atrium, and is associated with atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary congestion, and heart failure [3]. Therefore, VC is associated with increased cardiovascular (CV) and overall mortality, especially when VC progresses. In ESKD patients on maintenance hemodialysis (MHD), a higher degree of VC and an increased number of cardiac VCs are also associated with higher overall and CV mortality [4].

【Introduction · S0001-p1】Valve calcification (VC) is characterized by the gradual fibro-calcific remodeling and thickening of the valve leaflets [1]. The pathophysiology of VC is complex, influenced by traditional risk factors such as age, sex, smoking, and comorbidities like hypertension or diabetes mellitus. In patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), inflammation, malnutrition, and calcium-phosphorus metabolism disorders play significant roles in vascular or soft tissue calcification. The prevalence of VC among ESKD patients is approximately 31.7%, with risk factors including long dialysis vintages, elevated serum calcium level, high blood pressure, diabetes, and reduced serum albumin level [2]. Aortic VC leads to left ventricular outflow obstruction, increasing ventricular workload and oxygen consumption and ultimately causing myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis, while mitral VC causes dilation of the left atrium, and is associated with atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary congestion, and heart failure [3]. Therefore, VC is associated with increased cardiovascular (CV) and overall mortality, especially when VC progresses. In ESKD patients on maintenance hemodialysis (MHD), a higher degree of VC and an increased number of cardiac VCs are also associated with higher overall and CV mortality [4].

【Introduction · S0001-p2】The cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) is a noninvasive and easily obtainable parameter, which represents the overall cardiac silhouette on a chest posteroanterior (PA) radiograph. It is commonly associated with left ventricular size; therefore, an elevated CTR is considered to be associated with left ventricular mass and may correlate with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) [5]. In addition, a CTR above the value of 0.5 is used to identify cardiomegaly. The prevalence of CTR ≥ 0.5 among ESKD patients undergoing dialysis is approximately 55% [6]. CTR is also a recognized prognostic factor in various conditions, including hemodialysis patients. A large prospective cohort study of nearly 3,500 individuals with a four-year follow-up revealed that a higher CTR is associated with an elevated risk of both CV and overall mortality in this population [7]. Patients were stratified based on a CTR cutoff of ≥ 0.5. This threshold is a widely accepted and long-standing radiographic criterion for identifying cardiomegaly on standard posteroanterior chest radiograph and has been consistently associated with adverse outcomes [8]. Furthermore, another study also indicated that ESKD patients with a CTR ≥ 0.57 have an even greater risk of CV and overall mortality [9].

【Statistical analysis · S0002-S2006-p2】Univariate Cox regression was used to estimate the crude hazard ratio (cHR) and the 95% confidence interval (CI) for MACEs, CV, and overall mortality. In the multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, variables including age, sex, weight, vintage, CAD, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, triglyceride, hemoglobin, and ACEIs/ARBs from Table 1, were adjusted to calculate the adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for outcome events across the four groups. The proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals, and no significant violations were observed. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22 for Windows (IBM Corp.). A two-sided p < 0.05 indicated significance.

【Association of VC and CTR with MACEs · S0003-S2002-p2】In univariate Cox proportional hazard regression, relative to those with no VC with CTR < 0.5, the cHRs of MACEs were 2.443, 2.702, 4.053 (95% CI, 0.956–6.244, 1.138–6.413, 1.757–9.349, respectively) in groups of no VC with CTR ≥ 0.5, VC with CTR <0.5, and VC with CTR ≥ 0.5. After adjustment for age, sex (model [1]) or age, sex, weight, vintage, CAD, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, triglyceride, hemoglobin, and ACEIs/ARBs (model [2]), those with VC with CTR ≥ 0.5 remained a significant risk factor of MACEs (aHR, 4.174, 2.787; 95% CI, 1.766–9.868, 1.140–6.817, respectively), which was shown in Table 2.

【Figure 1. · F0001】Figure 1. Flowchart of patient selection and grouping. A total of 345 maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients who underwent both echocardiography and chest radiography between October and December 2018 were screened. After excluding 33 patients using tunneled cuffed catheters, 312 MHD patients with functional arteriovenous access were included and categorized into four groups according to the presence of valve calcification (VC) and cardiothoracic ratio (CTR < 0.5 or ≥ 0.5).

【Figure 2. · F0002】Figure 2. Cumulative hazards of (a) major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), (b) cardiovascular mortality, and (c) all-cause mortality among four groups stratified by valve calcification (VC) and cardiothoracic ratio (CTR < 0.5 or ≥ 0.5) during follow-up. Curves were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by log-rank test. The number of patients at risk in each group is provided below the time axis.

【Table 1. · t0001】Table 1. Baseline characteristics of four groups of maintenance hemodialysis patients based on valve calcification and cardiomegaly.
